pages.lede: Security is the trade the layering charts forget: hours of standing still generate almost no heat, so kit that works for a moving trade fails on a gatehouse at 3am. The list below is built around the static problem.

blocks.h2: Standing still is a cold-weather sport
blocks.html:
A patrol officer walking generates several times the heat of one posted static — which is why the same jacket that overheats a groundworker leaves a gatehouse officer shivering. The static answer is more insulation than looks reasonable: a longline insulated parka over a mid-layer over a proper base layer, warm footwear with room for circulation (tight boots on cold concrete are a misery machine), and covered head and hands from the first cold hour.

The other half of the brief is looking like authority rather than trades: dark uniform colours, embroidered branding, and a silhouette that reads corporate. Where duties include traffic or car parks, a Class 2 vest goes over the lot — visibility and identity in one garment.

items.l: Half a size up for winter socks — circulation is insulation
A spare shirt rescues a spilled-coffee shift
Gloves that can't press a PTT button come off — and stay off

faq.q: What do security guards wear in winter?
faq.a: More than a moving trade needs: base layer, mid layer and a longline insulated parka, with warm loose-fitting footwear, hat and gloves — static posts generate almost no body heat, so the insulation has to do all the work.

faq.q: Do security officers need safety footwear?
faq.a: Depends on the site: gatehouse and retail posts usually suit cushioned occupational footwear (comfort first), while industrial sites with vehicle and goods movement often mandate a toe cap — S1 or the site's stated spec. The assignment instructions decide.

faq.q: Do security staff need hi-vis?
faq.a: Wherever duties meet vehicles — car parks, gatehouses, traffic marshalling — a Class 2 vest over the uniform is standard. It doubles as instant identification, which is half its value on a busy site.

pages.cardBlurb: Tunics or polos, gloves that survive chemicals, and the slip-rated shoes that matter more than anything else on the list.
pages.h1: Cleaner's kit: built around wet floors and chemicals.
pages.metaTitle: Workwear for Cleaners: The Kit List | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Kit for cleaning staff — slip-rated washable footwear first, chemical-appropriate gloves, tunic vs polo uniform, and knee protection for the floors nobody thinks about.
pages.lede: Cleaning kit gets bought as an afterthought and worn around the two most persistent hazards in any building: wet floors and chemicals. Get the shoes and the gloves right and the rest of the list is straightforward.

head: Item
Spec
Why
rows: The cleaner works ON the wet floor everyone else avoids
Bleach splash writes off pale cheap fabric

Skin contact with cleaning chemistry is a dermatitis plan
Floor-level work adds up across a career
Sustained wet work protects the uniform

blocks.h2: Shoes and gloves do the protecting
blocks.html:
Footwear is the serious purchase: cleaners spend their shift on the wet side of the warning cone, so a slip-rated occupational shoe with a washable upper isn't a comfort item — it's the primary PPE of the job. Gloves split by chemistry: thin disposable nitrile handles routine wiping; dilution, dosing and anything the safety data sheet flags gets EN ISO 374 chemical gauntlets. Repeated "just this once" bare-handed chemical contact is how cleaning teams end up with occupational dermatitis — barrier cream and after-work moisturiser are the unglamorous back-up that dermatology nurses would put on this list themselves.

Uniform-wise, colour-coded tunics or polos matched to the healthcare pattern suit contract cleaning in clinical and care settings; embroidered polos read better in offices and retail.

items.l: The chemical's data sheet names the glove — not the nearest box
Washable uppers need drying time; two pairs outlast three singles
Dermatitis caught early is manageable; ignored, it's career-changing

faq.q: What shoes should cleaners wear?
faq.a: Washable uppers with slip-rated (SR) soles and real cushioning — cleaners work standing on the wet floors everyone else walks around. Occupational styles without toe caps suit most cleaning; add a cap only where goods handling justifies it.

faq.q: What gloves do cleaners need?
faq.a: Two tiers: disposable nitrile for routine tasks, and EN ISO 374 chemical-resistant gauntlets for diluting, dosing and anything the product's safety data sheet flags. Repeated bare-hand chemical contact is the main route to occupational dermatitis in cleaning.

faq.q: Why do cleaning uniforms use colour coding?
faq.a: In clinical and care settings, colour-coded uniforms (and equipment) separate clean and dirty areas and identify contract staff at a glance — mirroring healthcare's infection-control conventions. In offices and retail it's simpler: an embroidered polo identifies the team.

pages.lede: Multi-drop driving is a hundred small weather transitions a day: warm cab, cold kerb, wet tail lift, repeat. Kit built for either climate fails at the boundary — the list below is built for the transition itself.

heroMeta.l: You are the brand at the door

blocks.h2: Dress for the kerb, not the cab
blocks.html:
The cab takes care of itself — it's heated. The exposure is the ninety seconds per drop outside, times a hundred: which is why the working uniform is a wicking layer plus a softshell, with a real waterproof stowed rather than worn. Sweating inside a rain jacket for a dry mile then chilling at the next drop is the classic multi-drop mistake.

Footwear carries the injury risk: tail lifts, wet metal steps and kerb edges are where delivery injuries actually happen, so a trainer-style boot with a genuinely grippy wet-rated sole (and a toe cap where cages and heavy parcels feature) is the considered buy. And since the driver is the only human the customer meets, embroidered, presentable kit is the brand — a point logistics employers increasingly spec for.

items.l: Low sun through a windscreen is a daily hazard, not an accessory question
Rain, coffee or a split bag — the doorstep doesn't care why
Evening rounds make the hi-vis layer non-optional, not seasonal

faq.q: Do delivery drivers need hi-vis?
faq.a: In depots and loading bays, almost always — and kerbside work at dawn, dusk and night makes a Class 2 vest or jacket the sensible default year-round. Many carriers mandate it as part of the uniform.

faq.q: What shoes are best for delivery driving?
faq.a: Trainer-style safety or occupational footwear with a genuinely grippy wet-rated sole — tail lifts, van steps and wet kerbs are the real hazard list. Add a toe cap (S1P style) where cages, kegs or heavy parcels are part of the round.

faq.q: What should multi-drop drivers wear in winter?
faq.a: Layer for the transition, not the extremes: wicking base, softshell mid, and a stowed waterproof for the worst drops. A hundred heated-cab-to-cold-kerb cycles punish both a big coat (sweat) and a thin one (chill) — the mid-weight layer system wins.

heroImage.alt: Courier in yellow hi-vis with a delivery bag

pages.cardBlurb: Seated in a draught all shift — the FLT-specific kit logic: visibility, seated warmth, and boots for the dismount.
pages.h1: Forklift driver kit: seated, draughty, visible.
pages.metaTitle: Forklift Driver Workwear: The Kit List | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Kit for FLT and counterbalance drivers — hi-vis that stays visible seated, warmth for dock draughts, S1P boots for the dismount, and cold-store truck kit.
pages.lede: Forklift work has a kit profile all of its own: seated (so trunk warmth beats mobility), permanently in vehicle lanes (so hi-vis is identity), and punctuated by dismounts onto concrete (which is where the boots earn their keep).

head: Item
Spec
Why
rows: Class 2 vest or bodywarmer, always on
The truck is visible; the driver on foot must be too
Seated warmth without sleeve bulk at the wheel
Docks run cold and draughty year-round
The step-down onto concrete, hundreds of times
Wheel, levers, and the occasional pallet fix
Heat leaves seated bodies from the top

blocks.html:
Dock levellers and open roller doors put FLT drivers in a permanent draught — and seated bodies can't walk themselves warm. The kit answer is core insulation that doesn't restrict arms: the gilet-over-sweatshirt combination is practically the trade uniform, with a wicking base layer underneath in winter rather than a bulkier coat on top. Cold-store trucks push the whole list into EN 342 territory — cab heaters help, but the picking aisles don't.

The dismount is the injury moment: hundreds of step-downs onto concrete per shift, often backwards, sometimes onto debris. Cushioned-heel S1P boots with real ankle support, laced properly, are the difference-maker — and the reason "trainers are fine, I'm sat down" misses the point of the job.

items.l: Scarves and loose hoods near masts and moving chains — same rule as machine shops
Boot soles clean of pallet-wrap film grip pedals as well as floors
Try trousers and gilets sitting down — that's the working position

faq.q: Do forklift drivers need hi-vis?
faq.a: Yes — the standing convention is a Class 2 vest or hi-vis bodywarmer worn whenever on site, because drivers spend their day in vehicle lanes and become pedestrians the moment they dismount. Many operations treat it as non-negotiable uniform.

faq.q: What boots are best for forklift driving?
faq.a: S1P with a cushioned heel and decent ankle support — the hazard isn't the seat, it's the hundreds of dismounts onto concrete. A puncture midsole covers warehouse debris; toe caps cover the pallet and load work between drives.

faq.q: How do forklift drivers keep warm in winter?
faq.a: Core-first: gilet over sweatshirt over a wicking base layer keeps the trunk warm without sleeve bulk at the controls. Docks are draught alleys, so windproofing matters as much as insulation — and cold-store trucks step the whole kit up to EN 342-rated gear.

blocks.h2: Everyday kit and tool-day PPE are two lists
blocks.html:
The everyday list is classic outdoor trade: base layers under fleece under a maintained waterproof, knee-protected trousers, and boots chosen for mud. The tool-day list goes over it: strimmers, blowers and hedge cutters add flying debris and sustained noise, so EN 166-rated eyes (a mesh visor for sustained strimming), ear defenders and gloves become mandatory kit rather than judgement calls. Chainsaw work is its own world with its own certified clothing — covered separately — and no amount of general landscaping kit substitutes for it.

Roadside and verge work quietly adds a third list: Class 2 minimum, Class 3 by the carriageway — grounds contracts put teams on kerbs far more often than the job title suggests.

items.l: S3 leathers plus wellingtons — winter grounds work is a wet trade
Keep leather-palm and coated pairs both in the van; they solve different days
Spare socks, gloves and a fleece in the van rescue more afternoons than any single garment

faq.q: What PPE do you need for strimming?
faq.a: Rated eye protection (EN 166 impact grade F, or a mesh visor for sustained work), ear defenders, gloves, sturdy trousers and boots — strimmers fling stones and wire at eye height and deliver a hearing-damaging noise dose over a working day.

faq.q: What trousers are best for landscaping?
faq.a: Heavyweight or ripstop work trousers with EN 14404 knee-pad pockets — planting, edging and paving all happen at knee height, and knee protection is the highest-value feature on the garment. Waterproof over-trousers cover the wet months.

faq.q: Do landscapers need hi-vis?
faq.a: For roadside verges, kerbside work and anywhere plant operates, yes — Class 2 as the baseline and Class 3 alongside live carriageways. Grounds maintenance contracts put teams next to traffic far more than the job title suggests.

blocks.h2: Why the KP's footwear outranks the chef's
blocks.html:
Kitchens injure people at the floor, and the KP owns the wettest floor plus the heaviest loads — the barrel-and-crate work that puts this role, unusually for hospitality, in toe-cap territory: an S2 washable shoe or boot rather than the O2 the rest of the brigade wears. Same slip rating, same washable upper, plus the cap the cellar run justifies.

The other KP-specific truth: everything gets wet, so everything must dry. Quick-dry synthetics under a PVC bib beat cotton whites at this station, gloves live in pairs (hot-wet grip for the washer, chemical gauntlets for the machine chemistry), and a spare dry top at the half is worth more than any premium garment. The chef-side wardrobe logic lives in what chefs wear — the KP list is its wet-weather sibling.

items.l: PVC wipes down and hangs dry — a soaked cotton apron is a bacteria farm
Washer chemicals and hot trays are different hazards — different gloves
The cheapest morale item in any kitchen

faq.q: What do kitchen porters wear?
faq.a: Quick-dry basics under a full-length PVC bib apron, hot-washable trousers, washable slip-rated footwear — with a toe cap (S2) where keg and crate work features — plus grip gloves for hot wet handling and chemical gauntlets for machine chemistry.

faq.q: Do kitchen porters need safety shoes?
faq.a: They're the strongest case in the kitchen: the wettest floors plus the heaviest handling (kegs, crates, deliveries). An S2 washable shoe adds the toe cap to the slip-rated washable spec the whole kitchen wears — the cellar run justifies it.

faq.q: What gloves for the pot wash?
faq.a: Two kinds: heat-tolerant rubber grip gloves for scalding wet trays and pans, and EN ISO 374 chemical gauntlets for handling dishwasher chemicals and degreasers. One pair doing both jobs does neither properly.

pages.lede: Clinical kit lists get written by uniform policies; this one is written by the shift. Twelve hours, mostly standing, bare below the elbows, everything washed hot after every wear — the items below are chosen against exactly that.

blocks.h2: Footwear and sets — get these right first
blocks.html:
Footwear decides the shift. Hard flooring for twelve hours is a repetitive-strain machine, and the spec that survives it is boring and right: washable upper (spills are clinical reality), slip-rated sole, genuine cushioning, and replaced insoles when they flatten. Many ward staff run two pairs alternated — cushioning recovers between shifts, exactly like the boot-rotation logic elsewhere on this site.

Sets are policy infrastructure: washing after every shift only works with three to five sets in rotation, and the under-issued wardrobe is the most common way uniform policy fails in practice. The employer-side view — laundering benchmarks, colour coding, support roles — lives in the healthcare sector guide; the pocket economy is the wearer-side detail worth shopping for: tunic and scrub designs differ wildly in pocket layout, and a shift's worth of gloves, tape, pens, phone and keys has to live somewhere.

items.l: Commute clothes and clinical kit stay separate — issue enough sets to make it real
Anything around a neck in clinical settings must give way when grabbed
Bare below the elbow includes the watch — pin-on fobs exist for exactly this

faq.q: What shoes are best for a 12-hour nursing shift?
faq.a: Washable uppers, slip-rated soles, closed toes and serious cushioning — then rotate two pairs so the cushioning recovers between shifts and replace insoles when they flatten. Footwear is the single biggest comfort decision in clinical work.

faq.q: How many sets of scrubs does a nurse need?
faq.a: Three to five, assuming a hot wash after every shift as policy requires. Fewer than three breaks the rotation the first time a shift gets messy — under-issuing sets is how uniform policies fail in practice.

faq.q: Why can't nurses wear wristwatches?
faq.a: Bare-below-the-elbow policies: forearms and wrists must be clear for effective handwashing and to avoid transfer between patients. The pin-on fob watch exists precisely to keep time-telling compliant.
